title: Constant Factors, Truncated Counters and Honest Slopes: The Number Field Sieve Is as Closed as the Quadratic Sieve
description: Three proposed per-instance levers on the number field sieve's L[1/3] cost are each closed by an elementary theorem: constant and bounded factors cannot change an L-exponent, rank–nullity forces a dependency counter capped at 60 to saturate, and ordered power-law slopes (1.242 < 1.819) cannot invert. Rank–nullity for relation matrices: the left nullity of an r×c matrix is at least the excess r−c, so a dependency count truncated at 60 equals 60 on every matrix with excess at least 60 (and already at excess 6 if nonzero dependency vectors over F2 are counted).

# Three Ways to Fool Yourself About Factoring — and Why the Number Field Sieve Stays Shut

*How a constant, a counter that stops at sixty, and two slopes closed every proposed shortcut through the fastest classical factoring algorithm.*

---

## The fortress

Every time you open a secure web page, your browser is betting on one belief: multiplying two large primes is easy, and undoing the multiplication is hard. Take $p = 1{,}000{,}000{,}007$ and $q = 1{,}000{,}000{,}009$. A pocket calculator gives $N = pq = 1{,}000{,}000{,}016{,}000{,}000{,}063$ in a moment. Going the other way, from $N$ back to $p$ and $q$, is much harder. For the 2048-bit numbers used in RSA, no known classical method can do it before the Sun burns out.

The best general method we have is the **number field sieve** (NFS). Its running time is written in a notation that looks strange at first:

$$L_N\!\left[\tfrac13,\, c\right] \;=\; \exp\!\Big(c\,(\ln N)^{1/3}\,(\ln\ln N)^{2/3}\Big), \qquad c = \left(\tfrac{64}{9}\right)^{1/3} \approx 1.923.$$

This sits between polynomial time (which would make factoring easy) and exponential time (which would make it hopeless). The exponent $\tfrac13$ is the first number that matters. The constant $c$ is the second. Since the early 1990s, cryptographers have treated "improving the NFS" as meaning one thing: lowering $\tfrac13$, or lowering $c$.

This article is about a research round that went looking for such an improvement. It tested three separate "channels" through which some property of the particular number $N$ might be used to speed up the sieve. All three were closed. The interesting part is *how*. In each case the evidence for a breakthrough failed for a reason simple enough to state as a short theorem. Those three theorems, plus a fourth about the structure of the algorithm, are worth knowing for anyone who measures algorithms.

## The setting: hunting for a lever

The earlier rounds of this program had studied the **quadratic sieve** (QS), an older cousin of the NFS, and found it "closed": nothing about a specific $N$ gives a speedup in the terms that dominate its cost. The NFS was the one family those rounds had said should *not* be lumped in with the quadratic sieve. In the quadratic sieve, the set of primes the algorithm works with (the "factor base") is fixed by $N$ itself, through a quadratic-residue condition. In the NFS, the algebraic half of the factor base is governed by an auxiliary polynomial of degree $d$, which describes an auxiliary number field. So the NFS's columns really are *decoupled* from $N$. Perhaps that freedom left room for a lever.

The round attacked along three lines. Its own built-in critics, the "refuters," were tasked with killing any claim that did not hold up. Here is what each channel claimed and why it failed.

## Channel one: a constant is not an $L$

The round's measurement of NFS behaviour produced exactly one positive result: a measured cost ratio for a modified procedure. The first problem was practical. Nobody could reproduce it. The data file did not record which $N$ or which smoothness bound $B$ were used, and no script on disk generated it. Rebuilt from scratch, the experiment gave a ratio of $0.9932 \pm 0.0122$ over four runs. In other words, no effect at all.

The second objection is deeper, and it would apply even if the number had been reproducible. Suppose a modification really did make the sieve run in $0.99$ times the time, or $0.5$ times, or $0.001$ times. Does that change the NFS's complexity?

It does not, and this can be stated precisely. Write $x = \ln N$ for the size of the number in natural-log units. Define the **$L$-scale**

$$\Lambda_\alpha(x) = x^{\alpha}(\ln x)^{1-\alpha}.$$

Say that a cost function $f$ has **$L$-exponent $(\alpha, c)$** if

$$\frac{\ln f(x)}{\Lambda_\alpha(x)} \longrightarrow c \quad\text{as } x\to\infty.$$

This limit is the invariant the literature reports when it says "the NFS has constant $1.923$." It behaves as you would hope:

> **Theorem (the ladder is well defined).** For $0<\alpha\le 1$, the function $L[\alpha,c]$ has $L$-exponent exactly $(\alpha,c)$, and the constant of any cost function, when it exists, is unique.

Now multiply by a constant $K>0$:

$$\frac{\ln(K f(x))}{\Lambda_\alpha(x)} = \frac{\ln K}{\Lambda_\alpha(x)} + \frac{\ln f(x)}{\Lambda_\alpha(x)}.$$

The first term is a fixed number divided by something that grows without bound, so it disappears.

> **Theorem (constant factors are invisible).** If $f$ is eventually positive and has $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c)$, then $Kf$ has the same $L$-exponent for every $K>0$. More generally, if $a \le g(x) \le b$ for positive constants $a,b$, then $g\cdot f$ has the same exponent.

The second version covers the case at hand exactly. A "speedup" quoted as $0.9932 \pm 0.0122$ is a factor trapped between two positive constants. Whatever it is, it cannot show up on the $L$-ladder.

The converse is just as sharp. A real improvement from $c$ to a smaller $c'$ is very large:

> **Theorem (genuine gains are superpolynomial).** If $c'<c$ and $0<\alpha\le1$, then $L[\alpha,c]/L[\alpha,c']$ eventually exceeds $x^d$ for *every* power $d$. Consequently no constant $K$ satisfies $L[\alpha,c] \le K\cdot L[\alpha,c']$ for all large $x$.

The proof is a single line. The ratio is itself an $L$-function, $L[\alpha, c-c']$, and $\exp\big((c-c')x^\alpha(\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\big)$ grows faster than $\exp\big((c-c')x^\alpha\big)$, which outgrows every polynomial.

So "constant-factor effect" and "$L[1/3]$ effect" are two completely separate categories. A finite set of experiments that shows a constant ratio is evidence for the first category and *never* for the second. The refuters ruled the positive result worthless *by category*, and the theorem says that ruling was correct.

## Channel two: the counter that stopped at sixty

Every sieve, QS and NFS alike, ends the same way. You collect "relations": numbers that factor completely over a small set of primes. You write each one as a row of exponents mod 2. Then you look for a set of rows that adds up to zero mod 2. Such a set multiplies to a perfect square on both sides of a congruence, and a gcd computation then splits $N$ with probability about one half.

The round's second channel looked at this linear-algebra step. A routine called `left_dependencies` was supposed to measure, instance by instance, how much work sparse elimination needs and how many dependencies it finds. Reading the code turned up a plain bug: **the routine breaks out of its loop after 60 dependencies.** Every operation count and fill-in figure was therefore read off a truncated run.

How bad is that? Linear algebra answers in two lines. Let $M$ be the relation matrix, with $r$ rows (relations) and $c$ columns (primes), over any field. Let the **left nullity** be the dimension of the space of vectors $v$ with $vM=0$, which is the number of independent dependencies.

> **Theorem (rank–nullity for relations).** $\operatorname{rank} M + \text{(left nullity)} = r$. Since $\operatorname{rank} M \le c$, the left nullity is at least the **excess** $r-c$. Over $\mathbb F_2$ the space of dependencies has exactly $2^{\text{nullity}}$ elements, so there are at least $2^{r-c}-1$ nonzero dependencies.

This is the basic guarantee of every sieve: collect more relations than primes and squares are certain to exist. It also shows what a capped counter does. If the reading is $\min(60, \text{nullity})$:

> **Theorem (saturation).** On every matrix with excess $r - c \ge 60$, the truncated reading is exactly $60$. Any two such matrices, of any shapes and from any $N$, give identical readings.

A real NFS run collects excess relations deliberately, so in the regime that matters the instrument returns the constant 60. It cannot distinguish one instance from another. It is like a thermometer whose scale stops at body temperature, used to look for fevers. The situation is worse still if the routine counted *dependency vectors* rather than independent dependencies. Since $2^6-1 = 63 > 60$, the cap is reached once the excess is just $6$.

## Channel three: the inversion that wasn't

The last headline from the sparse-algebra channel was an "inversion." The idea: as you collect more relations, the surplus of dependencies grows faster than the cost of the wider matrix, so extra consumption eventually pays for itself.

The refuters used the miner's own numbers. Over the measured range, the surplus grew by a factor of $7.94$ while the width grew by a factor of $5.30$. On a log–log plot, the slope of the surplus is

$$s = \frac{\ln 7.94}{\ln 5.30} \approx 1.242.$$

The width cost, by the miner's own fit, scales like $W^{1.819}$.

The two-point slope is the right estimator: on an exact power law $aW^s$ it returns $s$ exactly. The bracket $\tfrac65 < s < \tfrac54$ can be checked with integer arithmetic alone, because

$$7.94^4 \approx 3974.5 < 5.3^5 \approx 4181.9, \qquad 5.3^6 \approx 22164 < 7.94^5 \approx 31557.$$

So $s < 1.25 < 1.819$. Both quantities grow, and the cost grows faster. For power laws that settles the question:

> **Theorem (no inversion).** Let the surplus be $S(W)=aW^s$ and the cost $C(W)=bW^t$ with $a,b>0$ and $0<s<t$. Then both are increasing; the ratio $S/C = (a/b)W^{-(t-s)}$ is strictly decreasing and tends to $0$; and once $C(W_0)\ge S(W_0)$ at some width $W_0$, it stays so at every larger width.

There is no consumption level at which the curves cross back. The "inversion" exists in neither the data nor the mathematics.

## The structural reason: decoupling without excess

Why did all three channels close? The answer comes from the one thing that *is* different about the NFS.

The NFS starts by choosing a polynomial. The classical method is **base-$m$ selection**: choose $m$ with $m^d \le N < m^{d+1}$ and write $N$ in base $m$. The digits become the coefficients of a polynomial $f$ of degree $d$ with $f(m)=N$.

> **Theorem (base-$m$ selection).** If $m \ge 2$ and $m^d \le N < m^{d+1}$, the digit polynomial has degree exactly $d$, satisfies $f(m) = N$, and has every coefficient smaller than $m \le N^{1/d}$.

For our $N = 1{,}000{,}000{,}016{,}000{,}000{,}063$ and $d=3$, $m = 10^6$ and $f(X) = X^3 + 16000X + 63$. The sieve then looks for coprime pairs $(a,b)$ that make both $a - bm$ and the homogeneous norm $F(a,b)=\sum_i c_i a^i b^{d-i}$ smooth. The size of that norm is controlled by an elementary bound:

> **Theorem (norm bound).** If every $|c_i| \le M$ and $|a|,|b| \le U$, then $|F(a,b)| \le (d+1)\,M\,U^d$.

For a fixed degree, the factor $d+1$ is a constant, and by channel one it is invisible on the $L$-ladder.

The final step balances the degree. With $u = \ln U$ and $x = \ln N$, the log-sizes of the two sides combine to roughly $d\,u + x/d$. The AM–GM inequality settles it:

> **Theorem (degree balance).** For positive $u, x, d$: $\;d\,u + x/d \ge 2\sqrt{ux}$, with equality exactly when $d=\sqrt{x/u}$.

This variational principle produces the exponent $\tfrac13$ once $u$ is balanced in turn. It also shows that choosing $d$ cleverly for a particular instance can at best *reach* the balanced value, never go below it.

That is the full picture. The NFS's columns are governed by $d$ and not directly by $N$, so the decoupling is real and the round genuinely studied the NFS rather than the quadratic sieve under another name. But the decoupled quantities reach the cost only through a balance whose optimum is fixed, and through factors such as $d+1$ that are constants. There is no surplus in the factor base and no validated structural quantity that controls the elimination cost. **Zero factoring methods came out of the round. The NFS, like the QS, has no exploitable per-instance lever in the terms that dominate its cost.**

## Why a closed door is worth writing about

This might look like a report of failure. It is better read as a set of rules for anyone who measures algorithms, whether the subject is factoring, protein folding or training a neural network:

1. **Know which scale your claim lives on.** A ratio measured with error bars is a bounded factor, and bounded factors are invisible on any scale like $L[\alpha,c]$. To claim an asymptotic gain you need evidence that the ratio grows faster than every polynomial.
2. **Make sure your instrument can move.** A counter capped at $k$ returns $k$ on everything past the cap. If theory (here, rank–nullity) puts every interesting instance past the cap, the instrument measures nothing.
3. **Compare slopes honestly.** Two increasing power laws with different exponents never trade places twice. If the cost exponent is larger, the cost wins from some point on and keeps winning.

Each rule corresponds to a short theorem, and each is the kind of thing that can be checked before an experiment is run. The cryptographic protection on your browser is unaffected by this round, and now we know in detail why each proposed crack fails.

# Constant Factors, Truncated Counters and Honest Slopes: Closing the Per-Instance Channels of the Number Field Sieve

**Aristotle**

*October 2026*

---

## Abstract

We examine three proposed channels through which structure specific to an instance $N$ might yield an exploitable improvement to the general number field sieve (NFS) within the terms of its subexponential cost $L_N[1/3, (64/9)^{1/3}]$. The channels are (i) a measured cost ratio for a modified sieve, (ii) per-instance measurements of sparse $\mathbb F_2$ elimination in the congruence-of-squares stage, and (iii) a claimed "inversion" in which the dependency surplus outgrows the width cost of the relation matrix. Each is closed by an elementary theorem. (i) The $L$-exponent of a cost function is unique and does not change under multiplication by any factor bounded between positive constants, whereas a genuine improvement of the constant produces a superpolynomial ratio. Constant-factor effects and $L$-effects are therefore strictly separated, and a measured ratio $0.9932 \pm 0.0122$ belongs to the first class. (ii) By rank–nullity the left nullity of a relation matrix is at least its excess $r-c$, so a dependency counter truncated at $60$ returns the constant $60$ on every matrix of excess at least $60$, and already at excess $6$ if nonzero dependency vectors are counted. (iii) The two-point log–log slope of the surplus is $\ln 7.94/\ln 5.30 \in (6/5, 5/4)$, strictly below the width exponent $1.819$. For power laws with $0<s<t$ the surplus-to-cost ratio decreases strictly to $0$, so no inversion exists at any consumption level. We complete the picture with the structural facts behind the decoupling of the NFS factor base from $N$: base-$m$ polynomial selection, the homogeneous norm bound $|F(a,b)| \le (d+1)MU^d$, and the degree balance $du + x/d \ge 2\sqrt{ux}$ with its unique optimum. The decoupling is real but produces no excess. The conclusion is that the NFS, like the quadratic sieve, has no exploitable per-instance lever in its $L[1/3]$ cost terms as measured.

---

## 1. Introduction

The general number field sieve factors an integer $N$ in heuristic time

$$L_N\!\left[\tfrac13, c\right], \qquad L_N[\alpha, c] = \exp\!\Big(c\,(\ln N)^{\alpha}(\ln\ln N)^{1-\alpha}\Big), \qquad c = \left(\tfrac{64}{9}\right)^{1/3} \approx 1.923.$$

An improvement in this regime means lowering $\alpha$ or lowering $c$. Earlier work in the present program found the quadratic sieve (QS) closed: no per-instance structure of $N$ can be exploited in its paid $L[1/2]$ terms. The underlying reason is that the QS factor base is pinned to $N$ by the quadratic-residue condition $\left(\frac{N}{p}\right)=1$. The NFS was flagged as the one family to which this conclusion should not be extrapolated. Its algebraic factor base consists of prime ideals of degree one in an auxiliary number field $\mathbb Q(\theta)$, $f(\theta)=0$, of degree $d$. The column set is therefore governed by $d$ (and by $f$) rather than by $N$ directly.

This paper gives the adjudicated account of a round that tested whether this decoupling leaves an exploitable lever. Three channels were proposed, and adversarial review rejected all three. Our contribution is to show that each rejection rests on a short, fully rigorous mathematical statement, which we state and prove below:

1. **Constant factors are $L$-invisible** (Section 3). This is the theorem behind rejecting the measurement channel's single positive result as a constant-factor effect.
2. **Truncated dependency counts saturate** (Section 4). This is the theorem behind rejecting the sparse-linear-algebra experiment on instrument validity.
3. **Power laws with ordered exponents do not invert** (Section 5). This is the theorem behind rejecting the "inversion" headline using the experiment's own slopes.
4. **Decoupling without excess** (Section 6). These are the structural facts that explain why all three channels close.

We stress the empirical background, which the theorems complement rather than replace. The measurement channel's positive result could not be reproduced: the stored data recorded neither $N$ nor the smoothness bound $B$, and no generating procedure was available. A from-scratch rebuild produced a ratio of $0.9932 \pm 0.0122$ over $n = 4$ runs, consistent with no effect. The sparse-algebra routine was found to break out of its row loop after $60$ dependencies. The theorems below show that even under the most favourable reading of the data, none of the claims could have supported an $L[1/3]$ improvement.

### 1.1 Notation

Throughout, $x = \ln N > 0$ denotes the size variable. For $0 < \alpha \le 1$ and $c \in \mathbb R$ we write

$$L[\alpha, c](x) = \exp\!\big(c\, x^{\alpha} (\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\big), \qquad \Lambda_\alpha(x) = x^{\alpha}(\ln x)^{1-\alpha},$$

so that $\ln L[\alpha,c](x) = c\,\Lambda_\alpha(x)$. "Eventually" means "for all sufficiently large $x$."

---

## 2. The $L$-exponent

**Definition 2.1 ($L$-exponent).** A function $f:\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ *has $L$-exponent $(\alpha, c)$* if

$$\lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{\ln f(x)}{\Lambda_\alpha(x)} = c.$$

This is the invariant reported in the factoring literature. For instance, "the NFS has constant $(64/9)^{1/3}$ at $\alpha = 1/3$."

**Lemma 2.2 (the scale diverges).** For $0 < \alpha \le 1$, $\Lambda_\alpha(x) \to \infty$.

*Proof.* For $x \ge e$ we have $\ln x \ge 1$. Since $1 - \alpha \ge 0$, this gives $(\ln x)^{1-\alpha} \ge 1$, hence $\Lambda_\alpha(x) \ge x^{\alpha} \to \infty$. $\square$

**Proposition 2.3 ($L$-functions have the expected exponent; uniqueness).** For $0<\alpha\le 1$ and any $c$, $L[\alpha,c]$ has $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c)$. If $f$ has $L$-exponents $(\alpha,c)$ and $(\alpha,c')$, then $c = c'$.

*Proof.* Once $\Lambda_\alpha(x) > 0$, which holds eventually by Lemma 2.2, the quotient $\ln L[\alpha,c](x)/\Lambda_\alpha(x) = c$ is constant. Uniqueness is uniqueness of limits in $\mathbb R$. $\square$

---

## 3. Channel 1: constant factors are invisible to the $L$-ladder

### 3.1 Invisibility

**Theorem 3.1 (constant factors are invisible).** Let $0<\alpha\le1$ and $K>0$. If $f$ is eventually positive and has $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c)$, then $x \mapsto K f(x)$ has $L$-exponent $(\alpha, c)$.

*Proof.* Eventually $f(x) > 0$ and $\Lambda_\alpha(x) > 0$, and on that range

$$\frac{\ln(Kf(x))}{\Lambda_\alpha(x)} = \frac{\ln K}{\Lambda_\alpha(x)} + \frac{\ln f(x)}{\Lambda_\alpha(x)}.$$

The first term tends to $0$ by Lemma 2.2 and the second tends to $c$. $\square$

**Theorem 3.2 (bounded factors are invisible).** Let $0<\alpha\le1$ and $0<a$. Suppose $f$ is eventually positive with $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c)$, and $g$ eventually satisfies $a \le g(x) \le b$. Then $x\mapsto g(x)f(x)$ has $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c)$.

*Proof.* Eventually $\ln a/\Lambda_\alpha \le \ln g/\Lambda_\alpha \le \ln b/\Lambda_\alpha$, using monotonicity of $\ln$ and positivity of $\Lambda_\alpha$. Both bounds tend to $0$, so the squeeze theorem gives $\ln g(x)/\Lambda_\alpha(x) \to 0$. Adding $\ln f/\Lambda_\alpha \to c$ completes the proof. $\square$

Theorem 3.2 is the precise form needed for experimental data. A measured "speedup ratio" reported as $\rho \pm \sigma$ with $\rho - \sigma > 0$ describes a perturbation confined between positive constants. In particular the rebuilt figure $0.9932 \pm 0.0122$, and any reproducible value of this kind, leaves the $L$-exponent unchanged.

### 3.2 Genuine gains are superpolynomial

**Lemma 3.3.** $L[\alpha,c](x)/L[\alpha,c'](x) = L[\alpha, c-c'](x)$.

*Proof.* Subtract the exponents. $\square$

**Theorem 3.4 (a genuine $L$-gain is superpolynomial).** Let $0<\alpha\le1$, $c' < c$, and $d \in \mathbb R$. Then

$$\frac{L[\alpha,c](x)/L[\alpha,c'](x)}{x^{d}} \longrightarrow \infty.$$

*Proof.* Let $\delta = c - c' > 0$. For $x \ge e$, $(\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\ge 1$, so by Lemma 3.3

$$\frac{L[\alpha,\delta](x)}{x^d} \;\ge\; \frac{e^{\delta x^\alpha}}{(x^{\alpha})^{d/\alpha}}.$$

Substitute $y = x^\alpha \to \infty$. The right-hand side becomes $e^{\delta y}/y^{d/\alpha}$, which tends to infinity because exponentials dominate powers. $\square$

**Corollary 3.5 (separation of categories).** If $0<\alpha\le1$ and $c'<c$, then for no real $K$ does $L[\alpha,c](x) \le K\, L[\alpha,c'](x)$ hold eventually.

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 3.4 with $d = 0$. Eventually the ratio exceeds $K$, which contradicts the inequality at any point where both hold. $\square$

**Corollary 3.6 (the rejection of the measurement channel, as a theorem).** Let $0<\alpha\le1$, $K>0$ and $c' \ne c$. Then $K\cdot L[\alpha,c]$ has $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c)$ and does **not** have $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c')$.

*Proof.* Combine Proposition 2.3, Theorem 3.1 and uniqueness. $\square$

**Interpretation.** Constant-factor effects and $L$-constant effects are disjoint classes. A constant factor never moves $c$. A move of $c$ is never bounded by any constant factor, since it grows faster than every power of $\ln N$. A finite set of measurements showing a ratio near a constant therefore cannot be evidence of an $L[1/3]$ improvement, regardless of the value of the constant. This is exactly the category that the task specification declared worthless.

---

## 4. Channel 2: the truncated dependency counter

### 4.1 Rank–nullity for relation matrices

Let $K$ be a field and $M \in K^{r\times c}$ the relation matrix: one row per relation, one column per factor-base element. In the sieve setting $K = \mathbb F_2$ and the entries are exponents mod $2$.

**Definition 4.1.** The *left kernel* of $M$ is $\{v \in K^r : vM = 0\}$. The *left nullity* $\nu(M)$ is its dimension, which is the number of independent dependencies that Gaussian elimination finds. The *excess* is $r - c$ (truncated at $0$).

**Theorem 4.2 (rank–nullity for relations).** $\operatorname{rank}M + \nu(M) = r$. Consequently $\nu(M) \ge r - c$.

*Proof.* Apply rank–nullity to the linear map $v \mapsto vM$ from $K^r$, which is the map $M^{\mathsf T}$. Its image has dimension $\operatorname{rank}M^{\mathsf T} = \operatorname{rank}M \le c$. $\square$

**Corollary 4.3 (counting over $\mathbb F_2$).** If $K=\mathbb F_2$, the left kernel has exactly $2^{\nu(M)}$ elements. Hence there are at least $2^{r-c}-1$ nonzero dependencies.

*Proof.* A $\nu$-dimensional $\mathbb F_2$-space has $2^\nu$ elements. Combine with Theorem 4.2 and monotonicity of $2^{(\cdot)}$. $\square$

Theorem 4.2 is the basic guarantee of every congruence-of-squares method, QS and NFS alike. Once relations outnumber primes, dependencies are certain to exist, and each yields a congruence $X^2 \equiv Y^2 \pmod N$ (in the NFS, after the square root in the number field).

### 4.2 Saturation of a capped reading

**Definition 4.4.** For $k \in \mathbb N$, the *$k$-truncated reading* of a count $n$ is $\tau_k(n) = \min(k,n)$.

**Theorem 4.5 (saturation).** If $k \le r - c$, then $\tau_k(\nu(M)) = k$.

*Proof.* By Theorem 4.2, $\nu(M) \ge r-c \ge k$. $\square$

**Corollary 4.6 (blindness).** For matrices $M\in K^{r\times c}$ and $M'\in K^{r'\times c'}$ with $k \le r-c$ and $k \le r'-c'$, $\tau_k(\nu(M)) = \tau_k(\nu(M'))$. Moreover $\tau_k$ is not injective: $\tau_k(k) = \tau_k(k+1)$.

**Corollary 4.7 (the observed instance).** For every $M \in \mathbb F_2^{r\times c}$ with $r - c \ge 60$, $\tau_{60}(\nu(M)) = 60$.

**Corollary 4.8 (vector-count variant).** If the routine counts nonzero dependency *vectors* rather than independent dependencies, then for every $M\in\mathbb F_2^{r\times c}$ with $r - c \ge 6$,

$$\tau_{60}\big(\#\{v\ne 0: vM=0\}\big) = 60.$$

*Proof.* By Corollary 4.3 the count is at least $2^{6}-1 = 63 \ge 60$. $\square$

**Interpretation.** NFS runs deliberately oversample relations, because a positive excess is needed to guarantee dependencies (Theorem 4.2). In that regime a counter capped at $60$ is a constant function of the instance. Every derived per-instance quantity read off the truncated run, including operation counts, fill-in and dependency yield, is therefore measured on an artificially terminated computation. Such quantities cannot carry per-instance structure. This proves the rejection on instrument validity. It does not prove that untruncated measurements would carry no structure. That question is taken up in Section 8.

An exploratory run on random sparse $\mathbb F_2$ matrices with $200$ columns and $12$ nonzeros per row illustrates the theorem. The observed nullity always satisfied $\nu - (r-c) \in \{1, 2\}$ in our samples, and the capped reading was $60$ for every excess at least $59$. These are illustrations only, not part of the argument.

---

## 5. Channel 3: no inversion

The third claim was that the dependency surplus $S$ grows faster with matrix width $W$ than the elimination cost $C$, so that the surplus "pays for" wider matrices beyond some point. Over the measured range the surplus grew by a factor of $7.94$ while the width grew by a factor of $5.30$. The cost was fitted as $C \sim W^{1.819}$.

### 5.1 The estimator

**Definition 5.1.** The two-point log–log slope is $\displaystyle \sigma(W_1,W_2;S_1,S_2) = \frac{\ln(S_2/S_1)}{\ln(W_2/W_1)}$.

**Proposition 5.2 (consistency).** If $a>0$, $W_1,W_2>0$, $W_1\ne W_2$, then $\sigma(W_1,W_2; aW_1^s, aW_2^s) = s$.

*Proof.* $aW_2^s/(aW_1^s) = (W_2/W_1)^s$, and $\ln(q^s) = s\ln q$ with $\ln q \ne 0$. $\square$

### 5.2 Bracketing the surplus slope

Let $s^\ast = \ln 7.94/\ln 5.30$ and $t^\ast = 1.819$.

**Proposition 5.3.** $\tfrac65 < s^\ast < \tfrac54$. In particular $0 < s^\ast < t^\ast$.

*Proof.* Since $\ln 5.3>0$, the upper bound is equivalent to $4\ln 7.94 < 5\ln 5.3$, i.e. $7.94^4 < 5.3^5$. This holds: $3974.50\ldots < 4181.95\ldots$. The lower bound is equivalent to $5.3^6 < 7.94^5$, i.e. $22164.3\ldots < 31557.4\ldots$. Both are finite rational comparisons. $\square$

Numerically $s^\ast = 1.24237\ldots$.

### 5.3 Ordered power laws never invert

**Theorem 5.4 (no inversion).** Let $a,b>0$ and $0<s<t$. Put $S(W) = aW^s$ and $C(W)=bW^t$ for $W>0$. Then:

1. $S$ and $C$ are strictly increasing;
2. $S/C$ is strictly decreasing;
3. if $S(W_0)\le C(W_0)$ for some $W_0>0$, then $S(W)\le C(W)$ for all $W\ge W_0$;
4. $S(W)/C(W)\to 0$ as $W\to\infty$.

*Proof.* (1) follows from positivity of the exponents. For (2), $S/C = (a/b)W^{-(t-s)}$ with $t-s>0$. Statement (3) follows from (2), since $S/C\le 1$ at $W_0$ and the ratio decreases afterwards. Statement (4) holds because $W^{-(t-s)} \to 0$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.5.** With $s = s^\ast$ and $t = t^\ast$, and any $a,b>0$, the surplus-to-cost ratio is strictly decreasing and tends to $0$.

**Interpretation.** Both quantities grow, the cost grows faster, and the crossover (if it occurs in range at all) happens exactly once, in the direction of cost dominance. The "inversion" is contradicted by the experiment's own numbers at every consumption level.

---

## 6. The structural boundary: decoupling without excess

We now explain why every channel closes, using the one feature that separates the NFS from the QS.

### 6.1 Base-$m$ polynomial selection

**Theorem 6.1 (base-$m$ selection).** Let $m\ge2$, $d\ge 0$ and $m^d \le N < m^{d+1}$. Let $f(X) = \sum_i c_i X^i$, where $(c_0, c_1, \dots)$ are the base-$m$ digits of $N$. Then:

* $f(m) = N$;
* $0 \le c_i < m$ for all $i$;
* $c_d \ne 0$ and $c_i = 0$ for $i > d$, so $\deg f = d$;
* $m \le N^{1/d}$ (for $d \ge 1$).

*Proof.* Evaluating the digit polynomial at $m$ reconstructs $N$, and every base-$m$ digit is below $m$. The bounds $m^d \le N < m^{d+1}$ say that $N$ has exactly $d+1$ base-$m$ digits, with the leading one nonzero. $\square$

*Example.* For $N = 1\,000\,000\,016\,000\,000\,063 = (10^9+7)(10^9+9)$ and $d = 3$ we get $m = 10^6$ and $f(X) = X^3 + 16000X + 63$. For $d=4$ we get $m=31622$ and $f(X) = X^4 + 3X^3 + 3384X^2 + 13068X + 29311$.

The polynomial, and hence the algebraic factor base, depends on $N$ only through $(m,d)$. All sizes are governed by $d$. This is the precise sense in which the NFS column set is decoupled from $N$, unlike the QS.

### 6.2 The homogeneous norm bound

**Theorem 6.2.** Let $d\in\mathbb N$, $c_0,\dots,c_d \in\mathbb Z$ with $|c_i|\le M$, and $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ with $|a|,|b|\le U$. Then

$$\Big|\sum_{i=0}^{d} c_i\, a^{i} b^{d-i}\Big| \;\le\; (d+1)\, M\, U^{d}.$$

*Proof.* By the triangle inequality, each of the $d+1$ terms satisfies $|c_i a^i b^{d-i}| \le M U^i U^{d-i} = MU^d$. $\square$

The factor $d+1$ is a constant for each fixed degree, so by Theorem 3.1 it is $L$-invisible.

### 6.3 The degree balance

In the heuristic analysis, the log-size of the quantities that must be smooth behaves like $du + x/d$, where $u = \ln U$ measures the sieve region and $x = \ln N$.

**Theorem 6.3 (degree balance).** For $u,x,d>0$,

$$d\,u + \frac{x}{d} \;\ge\; 2\sqrt{ux},$$

with equality if and only if $d = \sqrt{x/u}$.

*Proof.* Multiply by $d$. The difference is $d^2u - 2d\sqrt{ux} + x = (d\sqrt u - \sqrt x)^2 \ge 0$, which vanishes exactly when $d = \sqrt{x/u}$. A direct computation confirms that this value attains $2\sqrt{ux}$. $\square$

This AM–GM principle yields the exponent $1/3$ once $u$ is balanced against the smoothness probability in turn. It also shows that any instance-dependent choice of degree can at best *reach* the balanced value, never go below it.

### 6.4 Synthesis

The decoupling of the NFS from $N$ is genuine (Theorem 6.1). The quantities it controls enter the cost in only two ways: through constant factors such as $d+1$ (Theorem 6.2), which are $L$-invisible (Section 3), and through a balance whose optimum is fixed (Theorem 6.3). The factor base therefore has no degree-effect surplus. The only proposed per-instance handle on elimination cost was an instrument that is provably constant in the relevant regime (Section 4) and whose headline is contradicted by its own slopes (Section 5).

**Verdict.** As measured, the NFS has no exploitable per-instance lever in the $L[1/3]$ terms that dominate its cost. Zero factoring methods result. The NFS is as closed as the QS. The investigation did, however, genuinely address the NFS and not the QS in disguise, because its column set is governed by $d$.

---

## 7. Algorithms and computational illustrations

The arguments above suggest three simple diagnostics that we recommend applying before any claim of asymptotic improvement is made.

**Algorithm A (empirical $L$-constant).** Given costs $f(x_j)$ at sizes $x_j$, compute $\hat c_j = \ln f(x_j)/\Lambda_\alpha(x_j)$. Under a constant factor $K$, $\hat c_j - c = \ln K/\Lambda_\alpha(x_j)$, which decays like $x_j^{-\alpha}$. Under a genuine gain, the log of the ratio between methods grows like $\Lambda_\alpha$. Cost: $O(1)$ per sample.

**Algorithm B (instrument saturation check).** Before trusting a capped counter $\tau_k$, compute the excess $r - c$ (or $\log_2(k+1)$ for vector counts). If every instance of interest has excess at least $k$, the instrument is constant by Theorem 4.5. Cost: $O(1)$.

**Algorithm C (slope comparison).** Estimate $s$ and $t$ by two-point log–log slopes (Proposition 5.2). Certify the order by rational comparisons such as $7.94^4<5.3^5$ (Proposition 5.3). If $s<t$, conclude no inversion (Theorem 5.4). Cost: $O(1)$ arithmetic.

An illustrative computation of $\hat c$ for $f = K\cdot L[1/3, 1.923]$ gives the following values:

| bits of $N$ | $K=1$ | $K=1000$ | $K = 0.001$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | 1.92300 | 2.22277 | 1.62323 |
| 4096 | 1.92300 | 2.04546 | 1.80054 |
| $2^{20}$ | 1.92300 | 1.93655 | 1.90945 |
| $2^{40}$ | 1.92300 | 1.92308 | 1.92292 |

These illustrate Theorem 3.1. Even a factor of $1000$ is visible at cryptographic sizes as an apparent shift in $\hat c$, and this shift is an artefact that vanishes asymptotically. This is a practical warning: finite-size fits of $c$ cannot distinguish constant factors from constant improvements without the separation of Corollary 3.5.

---

## 8. Discussion and future work

**What the theorems do and do not say.** Sections 3–5 show that the three pieces of evidence offered for an NFS lever cannot support the claims made for them. They do not prove that no per-instance lever exists in principle. That would require a lower bound on factoring that is far out of reach. The verdict is the precise one stated: no lever in the $L[1/3]$ paid terms *as measured here*.

**Methodological lessons.** (a) State the scale on which a claim lives. On $L$-scales, bounded factors are invisible and genuine gains are superpolynomial. (b) Check that an instrument can vary. Rank–nullity predicts saturation before any run. (c) Compare exponents, not curves. Ordered power laws cross at most once.

**Open directions.**

1. *Polynomial-factor rigidity.* For $0<\alpha<1$, show that $g\cdot f$ has the same $L$-exponent as $f$ whenever $x^{-k}\le g(x)\le x^{k}$. The squeeze of Theorem 3.2 applies once one shows $\ln x/\Lambda_\alpha(x)\to 0$.
2. *Untruncated dependency counts.* For random sparse $\mathbb F_2$ relation matrices with $w$ nonzeros per row and excess $e\ge0$, show $\mathbb E[\nu] = e + O(1)$ uniformly in $c$. Then even untruncated counts carry only the excess. The lower bound is Theorem 4.2.
3. *Integer-degree gap.* Bound $\min_{d\in\mathbb N}(du + x/d) - 2\sqrt{ux}$ by $\tfrac u4(1+o(1))$, linking Theorem 6.3 to Section 3.
4. *Base-$m$ coefficient equidistribution.* For fixed $d$ and $N$ uniform in $[m^d, m^{d+1})$, study the distribution of the base-$m$ coefficients. The expectation is that they carry no per-instance excess beyond the scale $m$.

---

## 9. Conclusion

Three channels, three elementary theorems, one verdict. A constant is not an $L$. A counter that stops at sixty reads sixty. A slope of $1.242$ never overtakes a slope of $1.819$. Beneath all three lies the structural fact that the NFS's freedom from $N$ is channelled through a degree whose optimum is fixed by AM–GM. The number field sieve, like the quadratic sieve before it, offers no per-instance lever in the terms that dominate its cost.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Closing the Number Field Sieve channels: numerical companion.

Pure standard-library Python (no numpy needed).  Each section illustrates one
theorem of the paper "Constant Factors, Truncated Counters and Honest Slopes".

  1. The L-exponent of L[alpha, c] is c, and constant / bounded factors do not move it.
  2. A genuine improvement c' < c gives a superpolynomial cost ratio.
  3. Rank-nullity over GF(2): nullity >= excess, and a counter capped at 60 saturates.
  4. The two-point slopes 1.242 vs 1.819: no inversion.
  5. Base-m polynomial selection and the homogeneous norm bound.
  6. The degree balance d*u + x/d >= 2*sqrt(u*x).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. L-functions and the L-exponent
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def log_L(alpha: float, c: float, x: float) -> float:
    """log L[alpha, c](x) = c * x^alpha * (log x)^(1 - alpha), with x = log N."""
    return c * x ** alpha * math.log(x) ** (1.0 - alpha)


def L_scale(alpha: float, x: float) -> float:
    """The L-scale x^alpha (log x)^(1-alpha)."""
    return x ** alpha * math.log(x) ** (1.0 - alpha)


def empirical_L_constant(log_cost: float, alpha: float, x: float) -> float:
    """The quotient log(cost) / L-scale whose limit defines the L-constant."""
    return log_cost / L_scale(alpha, x)


def section_L_exponent() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("1. Constant and bounded factors are invisible to the L-exponent")
    print("=" * 76)
    alpha = 1.0 / 3.0
    c = (64.0 / 9.0) ** (1.0 / 3.0)
    print(f"GNFS constant c = (64/9)^(1/3) = {c:.6f}")
    rng = random.Random(44)
    print(f"{'bits':>8} {'x=ln N':>10} {'f=L':>10} {'f=1000*L':>10} "
          f"{'f=0.001*L':>10} {'f=g*L, g in [0.98,1.006]':>26}")
    for bits in [512, 1024, 4096, 2 ** 16, 2 ** 20, 2 ** 30, 2 ** 40]:
        x = bits * math.log(2.0)
        base = log_L(alpha, c, x)
        g = rng.uniform(0.9932 - 0.0122, 0.9932 + 0.0122)  # a measured "ratio" with error bar
        row = [empirical_L_constant(base + math.log(K), alpha, x) for K in (1.0, 1000.0, 0.001)]
        row.append(empirical_L_constant(base + math.log(g), alpha, x))
        print(f"{bits:>8} {x:>10.1f} " + " ".join(f"{v:>10.5f}" for v in row[:3])
              + f" {row[3]:>26.5f}")
    print("All columns converge to the same constant: the factor is L-invisible.\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Genuine L-gains are superpolynomial
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def section_superpoly() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("2. A genuine constant improvement c' < c beats every polynomial")
    print("=" * 76)
    alpha = 1.0 / 3.0
    c = (64.0 / 9.0) ** (1.0 / 3.0)
    c2 = 1.902  # an illustrative smaller constant
    print(f"c = {c:.4f}, c' = {c2:.4f}; ratio L[c]/L[c'] = L[c - c'] = exp((c-c') * scale)")
    print(f"{'bits':>12} {'log10 ratio':>14} {'log10 (ratio / x^3)':>22}")
    for bits in [10 ** 3, 10 ** 5, 10 ** 7, 10 ** 9, 10 ** 11, 10 ** 13]:
        x = bits * math.log(2.0)
        lr = (c - c2) * L_scale(alpha, x)
        print(f"{bits:>12} {lr / math.log(10):>14.3f} {(lr - 3 * math.log(x)) / math.log(10):>22.3f}")
    print("Eventually the ratio exceeds x^3 (and any x^d): no constant K can emulate it.\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. GF(2) rank-nullity and the truncated counter
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def gf2_rank(rows: List[int], ncols: int) -> int:
    """Rank over GF(2) of a matrix whose rows are encoded as integer bitmasks."""
    pivots: dict[int, int] = {}
    rank = 0
    for r in rows:
        v = r
        for bit in range(ncols - 1, -1, -1):
            if not (v >> bit) & 1:
                continue
            if bit in pivots:
                v ^= pivots[bit]
            else:
                pivots[bit] = v
                rank += 1
                break
    return rank


def random_sparse_relation_matrix(r: int, c: int, w: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    """r rows, c columns, each row with w random ones (exponent vectors mod 2)."""
    rows: List[int] = []
    for _ in range(r):
        mask = 0
        for col in rng.sample(range(c), w):
            mask |= 1 << col
        rows.append(mask)
    return rows


def truncate(k: int, n: int) -> int:
    """A counter that stops after k items."""
    return min(k, n)


def section_truncation() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("3. Rank-nullity over GF(2) and the counter that stops at 60")
    print("=" * 76)
    rng = random.Random(2026)
    c = 200
    print(f"{'rows r':>7} {'cols c':>7} {'excess':>7} {'nullity':>8} "
          f"{'trunc60(nullity)':>17} {'trunc60(2^null - 1)':>20}")
    for excess in [0, 3, 6, 20, 59, 60, 61, 80, 150]:
        r = c + excess
        M = random_sparse_relation_matrix(r, c, 12, rng)
        nullity = r - gf2_rank(M, c)
        assert nullity >= excess, "rank-nullity violated?!"
        vec_count = 2 ** nullity - 1
        print(f"{r:>7} {c:>7} {excess:>7} {nullity:>8} {truncate(60, nullity):>17} "
              f"{truncate(60, vec_count):>20}")
    print("nullity >= excess always.  Once excess >= 60 the capped reading is the constant 60;")
    print("if nonzero dependency VECTORS are counted, the cap bites already at excess 6 (2^6-1=63).\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Slopes: no inversion
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def loglog_slope(W1: float, W2: float, S1: float, S2: float) -> float:
    """Two-point log-log slope estimator."""
    return math.log(S2 / S1) / math.log(W2 / W1)


def section_slopes() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("4. Surplus slope 1.242 versus width-cost slope 1.819: no inversion")
    print("=" * 76)
    s = math.log(7.94) / math.log(5.30)
    t = 1.819
    print(f"surplus slope s = log 7.94 / log 5.30 = {s:.6f}")
    print(f"integer certificates: 7.94^4 = {7.94 ** 4:.2f} < 5.3^5 = {5.3 ** 5:.2f}  (s < 5/4)")
    print(f"                      5.3^6 = {5.3 ** 6:.2f} < 7.94^5 = {7.94 ** 5:.2f} (s > 6/5)")
    print(f"exact power law check: slope of 3*W^1.5 between W=2,9 -> "
          f"{loglog_slope(2, 9, 3 * 2 ** 1.5, 3 * 9 ** 1.5):.6f}")
    a, b = 5.0, 1.0
    print(f"{'W':>8} {'surplus a W^s':>15} {'cost b W^t':>14} {'ratio':>10}")
    for W in [1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 100, 1000, 10 ** 5]:
        S, C = a * W ** s, b * W ** t
        print(f"{W:>8} {S:>15.2f} {C:>14.2f} {S / C:>10.5f}")
    crossing = (a / b) ** (1.0 / (t - s))
    print(f"cost overtakes surplus at W = (a/b)^(1/(t-s)) = {crossing:.2f} and never falls back.\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Base-m selection and the norm bound
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def integer_root(N: int, d: int) -> int:
    """floor(N^(1/d)) computed exactly."""
    m = int(round(N ** (1.0 / d)))
    while m ** d > N:
        m -= 1
    while (m + 1) ** d <= N:
        m += 1
    return m


def base_m_digits(N: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """Base-m digits of N, least significant first."""
    out: List[int] = []
    while N:
        N, rem = divmod(N, m)
        out.append(rem)
    return out


def homogeneous_norm(coeffs: Sequence[int], a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """F(a, b) = sum c_i a^i b^(d-i)."""
    d = len(coeffs) - 1
    return sum(ci * a ** i * b ** (d - i) for i, ci in enumerate(coeffs))


def section_base_m() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("5. Base-m polynomial selection and the norm bound |F(a,b)| <= (d+1) M U^d")
    print("=" * 76)
    N = 1000000016000000063  # = 1000000007 * 1000000009
    for d in [3, 4, 5]:
        m = integer_root(N, d)
        assert m ** d <= N < m ** (d + 1)
        f = base_m_digits(N, m)
        assert sum(ci * m ** i for i, ci in enumerate(f)) == N
        assert len(f) - 1 == d and all(ci < m for ci in f)
        print(f"d={d}: m={m}, coefficients (const first) = {f}")
        M = max(f)
        U = 1000
        rng = random.Random(d)
        worst = 0
        for _ in range(2000):
            a, b = rng.randint(-U, U), rng.randint(-U, U)
            worst = max(worst, abs(homogeneous_norm(f, a, b)))
        bound = (d + 1) * M * U ** d
        print(f"      largest sampled |F(a,b)| = {worst:.3e} <= bound {bound:.3e}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Degree balance
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def section_degree_balance() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("6. Degree balance: d*u + x/d >= 2 sqrt(u x), equality iff d = sqrt(x/u)")
    print("=" * 76)
    u, x = 20.0, 700.0
    dstar = math.sqrt(x / u)
    print(f"u = {u}, x = {x}; optimum d* = {dstar:.4f}, minimum 2 sqrt(ux) = {2 * math.sqrt(u * x):.4f}")
    for d in [2, 3, 4, 5, 5.9161, 6, 7, 8]:
        val = d * u + x / d
        print(f"  d = {d:>6}: d*u + x/d = {val:9.4f}   gap = {val - 2 * math.sqrt(u * x):8.4f}")
    best_int = min(range(1, 50), key=lambda k: k * u + x / k)
    print(f"best integer degree = {best_int}; (bounding this integer-rounding gap in general is an open problem).\n")


def main() -> None:
    section_L_exponent()
    section_superpoly()
    section_truncation()
    section_slopes()
    section_base_m()
    section_degree_balance()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

def gf2_rank(rows: List[int], ncols: int) -> int:
    """Rank over GF(2) of a matrix whose rows are encoded as integer bitmasks."""
    pivots: dict[int, int] = {}
    rank = 0
    for r in rows:
        v = r
        for bit in range(ncols - 1, -1, -1):
            if not (v >> bit) & 1:
                continue
            if bit in pivots:
                v ^= pivots[bit]
            else:
                pivots[bit] = v
                rank += 1
                break
    return rank


def random_sparse_relation_matrix(r: int, c: int, w: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    """r rows, c columns, each row with w random ones (exponent vectors mod 2)."""
    rows: List[int] = []
    for _ in range(r):
        mask = 0
        for col in rng.sample(range(c), w):
            mask |= 1 << col
        rows.append(mask)
    return rows


def truncate(k: int, n: int) -> int:
    """A counter that stops after k items."""
    return min(k, n)


def section_truncation() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("3. Rank-nullity over GF(2) and the counter that stops at 60")
    print("=" * 76)
    rng = random.Random(2026)
    c = 200
    print(f"{'rows r':>7} {'cols c':>7} {'excess':>7} {'nullity':>8} "
          f"{'trunc60(nullity)':>17} {'trunc60(2^null - 1)':>20}")
    for excess in [0, 3, 6, 20, 59, 60, 61, 80, 150]:
        r = c + excess
        M = random_sparse_relation_matrix(r, c, 12, rng)
        nullity = r - gf2_rank(M, c)
        assert nullity >= excess, "rank-nullity violated?!"
        vec_count = 2 ** nullity - 1
        print(f"{r:>7} {c:>7} {excess:>7} {nullity:>8} {truncate(60, nullity):>17} "
              f"{truncate(60, vec_count):>20}")
    print("nullity >= excess always.  Once excess >= 60 the capped reading is the constant 60;")
    print("if nonzero dependency VECTORS are counted, the cap bites already at excess 6 (2^6-1=63).\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Slopes: no inversion
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def loglog_slope(W1: float, W2: float, S1: float, S2: float) -> float:
    """Two-point log-log slope estimator."""
    return math.log(S2 / S1) / math.log(W2 / W1)


def section_slopes() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("4. Surplus slope 1.242 versus width-cost slope 1.819: no inversion")
    print("=" * 76)
    s = math.log(7.94) / math.log(5.30)
    t = 1.819
    print(f"surplus slope s = log 7.94 / log 5.30 = {s:.6f}")
    print(f"integer certificates: 7.94^4 = {7.94 ** 4:.2f} < 5.3^5 = {5.3 ** 5:.2f}  (s < 5/4)")
    print(f"                      5.3^6 = {5.3 ** 6:.2f} < 7.94^5 = {7.94 ** 5:.2f} (s > 6/5)")
    print(f"exact power law check: slope of 3*W^1.5 between W=2,9 -> "
          f"{loglog_slope(2, 9, 3 * 2 ** 1.5, 3 * 9 ** 1.5):.6f}")
    a, b = 5.0, 1.0
    print(f"{'W':>8} {'surplus a W^s':>15} {'cost b W^t':>14} {'ratio':>10}")
    for W in [1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 100, 1000, 10 ** 5]:
        S, C = a * W ** s, b * W ** t
        print(f"{W:>8} {S:>15.2f} {C:>14.2f} {S / C:>10.5f}")
    crossing = (a / b) ** (1.0 / (t - s))
    print(f"cost overtakes surplus at W = (a/b)^(1/(t-s)) = {crossing:.2f} and never falls back.\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Base-m selection and the norm bound
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def integer_root(N: int, d: int) -> int:
    """floor(N^(1/d)) computed exactly."""
    m = int(round(N ** (1.0 / d)))
    while m ** d > N:
        m -= 1
    while (m + 1) ** d <= N:
        m += 1
    return m


def base_m_digits(N: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """Base-m digits of N, least significant first."""
    out: List[int] = []
    while N:
        N, rem = divmod(N, m)
        out.append(rem)
    return out


def homogeneous_norm(coeffs: Sequence[int], a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """F(a, b) = sum c_i a^i b^(d-i)."""
    d = len(coeffs) - 1
    return sum(ci * a ** i * b ** (d - i) for i, ci in enumerate(coeffs))


def section_base_m() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("5. Base-m polynomial selection and the norm bound |F(a,b)| <= (d+1) M U^d")
    print("=" * 76)
    N = 1000000016000000063  # = 1000000007 * 1000000009
    for d in [3, 4, 5]:
        m = integer_root(N, d)
        assert m ** d <= N < m ** (d + 1)
        f = base_m_digits(N, m)
        assert sum(ci * m ** i for i, ci in enumerate(f)) == N
        assert len(f) - 1 == d and all(ci < m for ci in f)
        print(f"d={d}: m={m}, coefficients (const first) = {f}")
        M = max(f)
        U = 1000
        rng = random.Random(d)
        worst = 0
        for _ in range(2000):
            a, b = rng.randint(-U, U), rng.randint(-U, U)
            worst = max(worst, abs(homogeneous_norm(f, a, b)))
        bound = (d + 1) * M * U ** d
        print(f"      largest sampled |F(a,b)| = {worst:.3e} <= bound {bound:.3e}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Degree balance
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def section_degree_balance() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("6. Degree balance: d*u + x/d >= 2 sqrt(u x), equality iff d = sqrt(x/u)")
    print("=" * 76)
    u, x = 20.0, 700.0
    dstar = math.sqrt(x / u)
    print(f"u = {u}, x = {x}; optimum d* = {dstar:.4f}, minimum 2 sqrt(ux) = {2 * math.sqrt(u * x):.4f}")
    for d in [2, 3, 4, 5, 5.9161, 6, 7, 8]:
        val = d * u + x / d
        print(f"  d = {d:>6}: d*u + x/d = {val:9.4f}   gap = {val - 2 * math.sqrt(u * x):8.4f}")
    best_int = min(range(1, 50), key=lambda k: k * u + x / k)
    print(f"best integer degree = {best_int}; (bounding this integer-rounding gap in general is an open problem).\n")


def main() -> None:
    section_L_exponent()
    section_superpoly()
    section_truncation()
    section_slopes()
    section_base_m()
    section_degree_balance()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Empirical L-Constant Estimation and Constant-Factor Discrimination
algorithms.description: Given measured costs (or cost ratios between two methods) at several input sizes x_j = ln N_j, the algorithm computes the empirical L-constants c_hat_j = ln f(x_j) / Lambda_alpha(x_j), where Lambda_alpha(x) = x^alpha (ln x)^(1-alpha). For a ratio between two methods it fits ln(ratio) = A + delta * Lambda_alpha(x) by least squares. The theory behind it: a constant factor K contributes ln K / Lambda_alpha(x) -> 0 to the L-constant, so it fits as A = ln K with delta = 0 and is L-invisible. A genuine improvement c -> c' makes the ratio itself an L-function L[alpha, c - c'], which fits as delta = c - c' > 0 and is superpolynomial. The cost is O(n) for n samples. This is the diagnostic that classifies a ratio such as 0.9932 +- 0.0122 as a constant-factor effect.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: sizes x_1..x_n, log-ratios r_1..r_n, exponent alpha
1. for j = 1..n: S_j <- x_j^alpha * (ln x_j)^(1-alpha)
2. (A, delta) <- least-squares fit of r_j = A + delta * S_j
3. if |delta| < tol: RETURN 'constant-factor effect, K = exp(A): L-invisible'
4. else: RETURN 'candidate L-gain delta' (must be confirmed by growth of r_j across sizes)
CORRECTNESS: ln(K*f)/S = ln K/S + ln f/S and ln K/S -> 0 (constant invisibility);
             L[c]/L[c'] = L[c-c'] grows faster than every x^d (superpolynomial separation).
algorithms.code:
import math
from typing import Sequence


def L_scale(alpha: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Lambda_alpha(x) = x^alpha (ln x)^(1-alpha), with x = ln N."""
    return x ** alpha * math.log(x) ** (1 - alpha)


def empirical_L_constants(log_costs: Sequence[float], xs: Sequence[float], alpha: float) -> list[float]:
    """c_hat_j = ln f(x_j) / Lambda_alpha(x_j); its limit is the L-constant."""
    return [lc / L_scale(alpha, x) for lc, x in zip(log_costs, xs)]


def fit_log_ratio(log_ratios: Sequence[float], xs: Sequence[float], alpha: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Least-squares fit  ln(ratio) = A + delta * Lambda_alpha(x).

    A constant factor K gives A = ln K, delta = 0 (L-invisible).
    A genuine improvement c -> c' gives A = 0, delta = c - c' (superpolynomial ratio).
    """
    S = [L_scale(alpha, x) for x in xs]
    n = len(S)
    ms, mr = sum(S) / n, sum(log_ratios) / n
    var = sum((s - ms) ** 2 for s in S)
    delta = sum((s - ms) * (r - mr) for s, r in zip(S, log_ratios)) / var
    return mr - delta * ms, delta


def classify_ratio(log_ratios: Sequence[float], xs: Sequence[float], alpha: float, tol: float = 1e-3) -> str:
    A, delta = fit_log_ratio(log_ratios, xs, alpha)
    if abs(delta) < tol:
        return f"constant-factor effect, K ~ {math.exp(A):.4f} (L-invisible)"
    return f"candidate L-gain, delta = c - c' ~ {delta:.4f} (needs growth across sizes)"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    xs = [b * math.log(2) for b in (512, 1024, 2048, 4096)]
    print(classify_ratio([math.log(0.9932)] * 4, xs, 1 / 3))
    print(classify_ratio([0.02 * L_scale(1 / 3, x) for x in xs], xs, 1 / 3))

algorithms.name: Rank–Nullity Saturation Test for Truncated Dependency Counters
algorithms.description: Every congruence-of-squares sieve ends with a sparse matrix M over F_2 (r relations by c primes). By rank–nullity, the left nullity is nu(M) = r - rank(M) >= r - c, and over F_2 there are 2^nu dependency vectors. A counter that stops after k dependencies therefore returns min(k, nu), which equals k for every matrix with excess r - c >= k. If it counts vectors, it saturates once 2^(r-c) - 1 >= k, which is excess 6 for k = 60. The algorithm computes the exact GF(2) nullity by bitmask Gaussian elimination in O(r c^2 / wordsize) and decides in O(1), before any experiment is run, whether a capped instrument can carry any per-instance signal.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: r, c, cap k, mode in {independent, vectors}
1. e <- max(r - c, 0)
2. if mode = independent: saturated <- (e >= k)
3. if mode = vectors: saturated <- (2^e - 1 >= k)
4. RETURN saturated   // if true, reading = k for EVERY such matrix
OPTIONAL exact nullity:
  pivots <- empty; rank <- 0
  for each row v: for bit b from high to low with v_b = 1:
      if pivot[b] exists: v <- v XOR pivot[b] else: pivot[b] <- v; rank++; break
  RETURN r - rank

algorithms.name: Certified Log–Log Slope Comparison (No-Inversion Test)
algorithms.description: To test whether a surplus S ~ a W^s can overtake a cost C ~ b W^t, estimate exponents by the two-point log-log slope sigma = ln(S2/S1)/ln(W2/W1). On an exact power law this returns the exponent exactly. The bracket of the slope is then certified by exact rational arithmetic: ln g / ln w < p/q iff g^q < w^p for g, w > 1. For the measured growth factors 7.94 and 5.30 this gives 6/5 < s < 5/4 < 1.819 = t. If 0 < s < t, the ratio S/C = (a/b) W^-(t-s) is strictly decreasing and tends to 0, and the crossing at W = (a/b)^(1/(t-s)) happens exactly once. No inversion is possible. All steps are O(1) arithmetic.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: growth factors g (surplus), w (width), cost exponent t, constants a, b
1. s <- ln g / ln w
2. certify s < p/q by checking g^q < w^p in exact rationals (and s > p'/q' by w^p' < g^q')
3. if 0 < s < t:
      W_cross <- (a/b)^(1/(t-s))
      RETURN 'S/C strictly decreasing to 0; cost dominates for all W >= W_cross; NO inversion'
4. else RETURN 'hypothesis fails'

algorithms.name: Base-m Polynomial Selection with Norm Bound and Degree Balancing
algorithms.description: The first step of the number field sieve. Given N and a degree d, compute m = floor(N^(1/d)) by exact integer root, check m^d <= N < m^(d+1), and read off the base-m digits as the coefficients of f with f(m) = N, deg f = d, and every coefficient < m <= N^(1/d). The homogeneous norm F(a,b) = sum c_i a^i b^(d-i) over the sieve box |a|,|b| <= U is bounded by (d+1) M U^d, a constant factor d+1 per fixed degree. The degree is chosen by the balance d u + x/d >= 2 sqrt(u x) (AM–GM), with the unique real optimum d* = sqrt(x/u). Complexity: O(log N) big-integer operations for the root and the digits.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: N, degree d (or u = ln U, x = ln N to choose d)
1. optionally d <- argmin over integers k of (k*u + x/k)   // real optimum sqrt(x/u)
2. m <- integer d-th root of N; require m >= 2 and m^d <= N < m^(d+1)
3. coeffs <- base-m digits of N (constant term first)
4. assert f(m) = N, deg f = d, max coeff < m
5. norm bound <- (d+1) * max|c_i| * U^d
6. RETURN m, f, norm bound

# Three Ways to Fool Yourself About Factoring

The **number field sieve** (NFS) is the fastest known classical algorithm for factoring large integers, and therefore the main threat to RSA. Its running time is

$$L_N\left[\tfrac13, c\right] = \exp\Big(c\,(\ln N)^{1/3}(\ln\ln N)^{2/3}\Big),\qquad c = (64/9)^{1/3}\approx 1.923.$$

A research round looked for a *per-instance lever*: some property of the specific $N$ that would lower $\tfrac13$ or $c$. It tried three channels. All three were closed, each by a short theorem. This page lets you see why.

<details><summary>Background: what is a "sieve" and why do squares matter?</summary>

Sieves look for many integers that factor completely over a small set of primes ("relations"). Writing each relation's exponents mod 2 gives a row of a matrix over $\mathbb F_2$. Any set of rows summing to zero gives a congruence $X^2\equiv Y^2 \pmod N$, and $\gcd(X-Y,N)$ is then a nontrivial factor with probability about $1/2$. The [quadratic sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_sieve) and the [general number field sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_number_field_sieve) both end this way. The difference between them is where the relations come from.
</details>

---

## Act I — A constant is not an $L$

The round's only positive measurement was a cost ratio. It could not be reproduced: a rebuild gave $0.9932\pm0.0122$. More importantly, even a reproducible constant ratio would not count. Define the **$L$-scale** $\Lambda_\alpha(x)=x^\alpha(\ln x)^{1-\alpha}$ with $x=\ln N$, and say $f$ *has $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c)$* when $\ln f(x)/\Lambda_\alpha(x)\to c$.

Try it: drag $K$ to $10^6$ and watch the empirical constant drift away and then come back.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

> **Theorem (constant and bounded factors are invisible).** If $f$ has $L$-exponent $(\alpha,c)$ and $a\le g(x)\le b$ with $a>0$, then $g\cdot f$ has the same $L$-exponent.
>
> **Theorem (genuine gains are superpolynomial).** If $c'<c$, then $L[\alpha,c]/L[\alpha,c']$ eventually exceeds $x^d$ for every $d$. So no constant $K$ can ever bridge an $L$-gain.

<details><summary>Proof sketch</summary>

$\ln(gf)/\Lambda = \ln g/\Lambda + \ln f/\Lambda$. Since $\ln a/\Lambda\le\ln g/\Lambda\le\ln b/\Lambda$ and both bounds tend to $0$ (because $\Lambda_\alpha(x)\ge x^\alpha\to\infty$ for $x\ge e$), the squeeze theorem kills the first term. For the second theorem, $L[c]/L[c']=L[c-c']\ge e^{(c-c')x^\alpha}$, and exponentials beat powers.
</details>

{{visualization:0}}

To apply this to data, fit $\ln(\text{ratio}) = A + \delta\,\Lambda_\alpha(x)$. A constant factor has $\delta = 0$:

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## Act II — The counter that stops at sixty

The sparse-algebra experiment used a routine that **stops after 60 dependencies**. Is that a small flaw or a fatal one? Rank–nullity decides.

> **Theorem (rank–nullity for relations).** For an $r\times c$ relation matrix, $\operatorname{rank}M+\nu(M)=r$, so the number of independent dependencies satisfies $\nu(M)\ge r-c$. Over $\mathbb F_2$ there are exactly $2^{\nu}$ dependency vectors.
>
> **Theorem (saturation).** If $r-c\ge k$, the truncated reading $\min(k,\nu(M))$ equals $k$. With $k=60$, every NFS run with excess $\ge 60$ reads exactly $60$. Counting vectors, the cap is reached at excess $6$, since $2^6-1=63$.

Run the laboratory below. The green curve hugs the diagonal from above, and the yellow instrument goes flat.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details><summary>Why this kills the channel, and what it does not prove</summary>

The NFS collects excess relations on purpose, because rank–nullity only guarantees dependencies when $r>c$. In exactly that regime the instrument is a constant function of the instance, so every operation count or fill figure read off the truncated run carries no per-instance information. This invalidates the *instrument*. Whether an *untruncated* count could carry structure is a separate question; the conjecture is that $\mathbb E[\nu]=e+O(1)$, i.e. it carries only the excess.
</details>

{{visualization:1}}

{{algorithm:1}}

## Act III — The inversion that wasn't

The headline claim was that the dependency surplus outgrows the width cost. Using the miner's own numbers, the surplus grew $7.94\times$ while the width grew $5.30\times$, so

$$s=\frac{\ln 7.94}{\ln 5.30}\approx 1.242,\qquad \tfrac65<s<\tfrac54\quad(\text{since }7.94^4<5.3^5,\ 5.3^6<7.94^5),$$

while the cost scales like $W^{1.819}$.

> **Theorem (no inversion).** For $S=aW^s$ and $C=bW^t$ with $a,b>0$ and $0<s<t$: both increase, $S/C$ strictly decreases to $0$, and once $C\ge S$ at some width it stays so forever.

{{interactive_demo:2}}

{{algorithm:2}}

## The structural reason: decoupling without excess

Unlike the quadratic sieve, the NFS's algebraic factor base is governed by a polynomial of degree $d$, not directly by $N$. Base-$m$ selection builds it:

> **Theorem (base-$m$ selection).** If $m\ge2$ and $m^d\le N<m^{d+1}$, the base-$m$ digits of $N$ form a polynomial $f$ with $f(m)=N$, $\deg f=d$, and all coefficients $<m$.
>
> **Theorem (norm bound).** $|\sum_i c_ia^ib^{d-i}|\le(d+1)MU^d$ when $|c_i|\le M$ and $|a|,|b|\le U$. The factor $d+1$ is a constant and therefore $L$-invisible.
>
> **Theorem (degree balance).** $du+x/d\ge 2\sqrt{ux}$, with equality iff $d=\sqrt{x/u}$.

The decoupling is real, but what it controls enters the cost only through constants and through a balance whose optimum is fixed. There is no surplus to exploit. Use the second and third panels of the widget above to see this.

**Zero factoring methods. As measured, the NFS is as closed as the QS.** The NFS's column set is decoupled from $N$, but the decoupling yields no exploitable excess: no factor-base surplus and no validated per-instance lever on the sparse-elimination cost.

<details><summary>Three rules for anyone who measures algorithms</summary>

1. Know which scale your claim lives on. Bounded factors are invisible on $L$-scales.
2. Make sure your instrument can move. A capped counter returns its cap on everything past it.
3. Compare exponents, not curves. Ordered power laws cross at most once.

import Mathlib

/-!
# NFS closure, channel 1: constant factors are invisible to the `L[α, c]` ladder

Round 44's single "positive" NFS-measure result was ruled out (`refuteB`) because it is a
**constant-factor** effect, not an `L[1/3]` effect.  This file makes that verdict a theorem.

We work with the subexponential complexity function of the catalog,
`Lfun α c x = exp (c · x^α · (log x)^(1-α))` in the bit-size variable `x = log N`
(this is verbatim `FactoringBarriers.Lfun` from
`Catalog/Cryptography/FactoringBarriers/AsymptoticLadder.lean`; it is restated here only
so that this file is self-contained under the `Physics` library).

## The `L`-exponent

A cost function `f` *has `L`-exponent `(α, c)`* when
`log (f x) / (x^α (log x)^(1-α)) → c`.  This is the invariant the NFS literature reports
(`c = (64/9)^{1/3}` for the general NFS at `α = 1/3`).

## Main results

* `LExponent.Lfun`            : `Lfun α c` has `L`-exponent `(α, c)`;
* `LExponent.unique`          : the `L`-exponent constant is unique;
* `LExponent.const_mul`       : multiplying by any constant `K > 0` leaves it unchanged —
  **a constant-factor effect is invisible to the `L`-ladder** (the refuters' category);
* `LExponent.mul_of_bounded`  : more generally any factor bounded above and below by positive
  constants is invisible;
* `Lfun_ratio_superpoly`      : a *genuine* constant improvement `c' < c` produces a ratio
  `Lfun α c / Lfun α c'` which is superpolynomial;
* `const_factor_cannot_emulate_L_gain` : therefore no constant factor `K` can ever reproduce an
  `L`-constant improvement — the two categories are strictly separated.
-/

namespace Physics.NFSClosure

open Filter Real
open scoped Topology

/-- The catalog's subexponential complexity function `L_N[α, c]`, in `x = log N`. -/
noncomputable def Lfun (α c x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Real.exp (c * x ^ α * (Real.log x) ^ (1 - α))

/-- The `L`-scale `x^α (log x)^(1-α)`: the quantity whose coefficient is the `L`-constant. -/
noncomputable def Lscale (α x : ℝ) : ℝ := x ^ α * (Real.log x) ^ (1 - α)

/-- `f` has `L`-exponent `(α, c)`. -/
def LExponent (f : ℝ → ℝ) (α c : ℝ) : Prop :=
  Tendsto (fun x => Real.log (f x) / Lscale α x) atTop (𝓝 c)

/-- For `0 < α ≤ 1` the `L`-scale tends to infinity. -/
theorem Lscale_tendsto_atTop {α : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1) :
    Tendsto (Lscale α) atTop atTop := by
  refine tendsto_atTop_mono' atTop ?_ (tendsto_rpow_atTop hα)
  filter_upwards [eventually_ge_atTop (Real.exp 1)] with x hx
  have hx0 : (0:ℝ) < x := lt_of_lt_of_le (Real.exp_pos 1) hx
  have hlog : (1:ℝ) ≤ Real.log x := by
    have := Real.log_le_log (Real.exp_pos 1) hx
    simpa using this
  have hpow : (1:ℝ) ≤ (Real.log x) ^ (1 - α) := Real.one_le_rpow hlog (by linarith)
  have hxa : (0:ℝ) ≤ x ^ α := (Real.rpow_pos_of_pos hx0 α).le
  unfold Lscale
  nlinarith

theorem log_Lfun (α c x : ℝ) : Real.log (Lfun α c x) = c * Lscale α x := by
  unfold Lfun Lscale
  rw [Real.log_exp]
  ring

/-- `Lfun α c` has `L`-exponent exactly `(α, c)`. -/
theorem LExponent.Lfun {α c : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1) :
    LExponent (Lfun α c) α c := by
  unfold LExponent
  refine tendsto_const_nhds.congr' ?_
  filter_upwards [(Lscale_tendsto_atTop hα hα1).eventually_gt_atTop 0] with x hx
  rw [log_Lfun, mul_div_assoc, div_self hx.ne', mul_one]

/-- The `L`-constant is uniquely determined by the cost function. -/
theorem LExponent.unique {f : ℝ → ℝ} {α c c' : ℝ} (h : LExponent f α c)
    (h' : LExponent f α c') : c = c' :=
  tendsto_nhds_unique h h'

/-- **Constant factors are invisible.**  If `f` has `L`-exponent `(α, c)` and `K > 0`, then
`K • f` has the *same* `L`-exponent, provided `f` is eventually positive. -/
theorem LExponent.const_mul {f : ℝ → ℝ} {α c K : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1)
    (hK : 0 < K) (hpos : ∀ᶠ x in atTop, 0 < f x) (h : LExponent f α c) :
    LExponent (fun x => K * f x) α c := by
  unfold LExponent at *
  have hS := Lscale_tendsto_atTop hα hα1
  have hsmall : Tendsto (fun x => Real.log K / Lscale α x) atTop (𝓝 0) :=
    hS.const_div_atTop _
  have hsum := hsmall.add h
  rw [zero_add] at hsum
  refine hsum.congr' ?_
  filter_upwards [hpos, hS.eventually_gt_atTop 0] with x hx hSx
  rw [Real.log_mul hK.ne' hx.ne', add_div]

/-- **Bounded factors are invisible.**  Any multiplicative perturbation `g` with
`a ≤ g x ≤ b` for positive constants `a, b` leaves the `L`-exponent unchanged.  This covers
measured "speedups" with error bars, e.g. a ratio `0.9932 ± 0.0122`. -/
theorem LExponent.mul_of_bounded {f g : ℝ → ℝ} {α c a b : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1)
    (ha : 0 < a) (hpos : ∀ᶠ x in atTop, 0 < f x)
    (hg : ∀ᶠ x in atTop, a ≤ g x ∧ g x ≤ b) (h : LExponent f α c) :
    LExponent (fun x => g x * f x) α c := by
  unfold LExponent at *
  have hS := Lscale_tendsto_atTop hα hα1
  have hlo : Tendsto (fun x => Real.log a / Lscale α x) atTop (𝓝 0) := hS.const_div_atTop _
  have hhi : Tendsto (fun x => Real.log b / Lscale α x) atTop (𝓝 0) := hS.const_div_atTop _
  have hmid : Tendsto (fun x => Real.log (g x) / Lscale α x) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
    refine tendsto_of_tendsto_of_tendsto_of_le_of_le' hlo hhi ?_ ?_
    · filter_upwards [hg, hS.eventually_gt_atTop 0] with x hx hSx
      exact div_le_div_of_nonneg_right (Real.log_le_log ha hx.1) hSx.le
    · filter_upwards [hg, hS.eventually_gt_atTop 0] with x hx hSx
      exact div_le_div_of_nonneg_right (Real.log_le_log (lt_of_lt_of_le ha hx.1) hx.2) hSx.le
  have hsum := hmid.add h
  rw [zero_add] at hsum
  refine hsum.congr' ?_
  filter_upwards [hpos, hg, hS.eventually_gt_atTop 0] with x hx hgx hSx
  rw [Real.log_mul (lt_of_lt_of_le ha hgx.1).ne' hx.ne', add_div]

/-- The ratio of two `L`-functions with the same `α` is again an `L`-function. -/
theorem Lfun_div_Lfun (α c c' x : ℝ) : Lfun α c x / Lfun α c' x = Lfun α (c - c') x := by
  unfold Lfun
  rw [← Real.exp_sub]
  ring_nf

/-- **A genuine `L`-gain is superpolynomial.**  If `c' < c` and `0 < α ≤ 1`, the ratio
`Lfun α c / Lfun α c'` eventually exceeds every power `x ^ d` of the bit-size. -/
theorem Lfun_ratio_superpoly {α c c' : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1) (hcc : c' < c)
    (d : ℝ) : Tendsto (fun x => (Lfun α c x / Lfun α c' x) / x ^ d) atTop atTop := by
  have hδ : 0 < c - c' := by linarith
  have hcomp : Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => Real.exp ((c - c') * x) / x ^ (d / α)) atTop atTop :=
    tendsto_exp_mul_div_rpow_atTop (d / α) (c - c') hδ
  have hrp : Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => x ^ α) atTop atTop := tendsto_rpow_atTop hα
  refine tendsto_atTop_mono' atTop ?_ (hcomp.comp hrp)
  filter_upwards [eventually_ge_atTop (Real.exp 1)] with x hx
  have hx0 : (0:ℝ) < x := lt_of_lt_of_le (Real.exp_pos 1) hx
  have hlog : (1:ℝ) ≤ Real.log x := by
    have := Real.log_le_log (Real.exp_pos 1) hx
    simpa using this
  have hpow : (1:ℝ) ≤ (Real.log x) ^ (1 - α) := Real.one_le_rpow hlog (by linarith)
  have hxa : (0:ℝ) ≤ x ^ α := (Real.rpow_pos_of_pos hx0 α).le
  have hxd : (x ^ α) ^ (d / α) = x ^ d := by
    rw [← Real.rpow_mul hx0.le, mul_div_cancel₀ d hα.ne']
  simp only [Function.comp, hxd, Lfun_div_Lfun]
  have hpd : (0:ℝ) < x ^ d := Real.rpow_pos_of_pos hx0 d
  gcongr
  unfold Lfun
  apply Real.exp_le_exp.mpr
  nlinarith [mul_nonneg hδ.le hxa]

/-- **Separation of categories.**  For `c' < c` no constant factor `K` turns the cheaper
cost `Lfun α c'` into something that dominates `Lfun α c`: a constant-factor effect can never
emulate (or be mistaken for) an `L`-constant improvement. -/
theorem const_factor_cannot_emulate_L_gain {α c c' : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1)
    (hcc : c' < c) (K : ℝ) :
    ¬ ∀ᶠ x in atTop, Lfun α c x ≤ K * Lfun α c' x := by
  intro hK
  have h0 := Lfun_ratio_superpoly hα hα1 hcc 0
  have hbig := h0.eventually_gt_atTop K
  obtain ⟨x, h1, h2⟩ := (hK.and hbig).exists
  have hL : 0 < Lfun α c' x := Real.exp_pos _
  rw [Real.rpow_zero, div_one, lt_div_iff₀ hL] at h2
  linarith

/-- **Refuter B, as a theorem.**  Suppose an "improved" NFS cost is `K * Lfun α c` for a
constant `K > 0` (a constant-factor effect).  Then its `L`-exponent is still exactly `c`; in
particular it is *not* the `L`-exponent of any genuinely improved constant `c' ≠ c`. -/
theorem constant_factor_effect_has_no_L_gain {α c c' K : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1)
    (hK : 0 < K) (hcc : c' ≠ c) :
    LExponent (fun x => K * Lfun α c x) α c ∧
      ¬ LExponent (fun x => K * Lfun α c x) α c' := by
  have h := (LExponent.Lfun (c := c) hα hα1).const_mul hα hα1 hK
    (Eventually.of_forall fun x => Real.exp_pos _)
  exact ⟨h, fun h' => hcc (h.unique h').symm⟩

end Physics.NFSClosure

import Mathlib

/-!
# NFS closure, channel 2: the truncated `left_dependencies` instrument saturates

Round 44's sparse-linear-algebra experiment was killed on **instrument validity**
(`refuteA`): its routine `left_dependencies` breaks out of the row loop after `60`
dependencies, so every downstream quantity is read off a truncated run.

This file proves *why* such an instrument cannot carry a per-instance signal.

* `excess_le_leftNullity` : for a relation matrix `M` over any field, with `r` relations
  (rows) and `c` factor-base primes (columns), the space of left dependencies has dimension
  at least `r - c` (rank–nullity).  Over `𝔽₂` this is the congruence-of-squares guarantee of
  every sieve (QS **and** NFS).
* `card_leftKernel_GF2` : over `𝔽₂` the left kernel has exactly `2 ^ nullity` elements.
* `truncated_reading_saturates` : a reading truncated at a cap `k` equals `k` on **every**
  matrix whose excess `r - c` is at least `k`; with `k = 60` and any NFS run collecting
  `60` more relations than primes, the reading is the constant `60`.
* `truncated_reading_blind` : two such instances are indistinguishable by the instrument,
  however different their actual dependency spaces — so the reading cannot be a lever.
* `truncated_vector_count_saturates` : if instead every nonzero dependency vector is
  counted, the cap `60` is already reached at excess `6`, since `2^6 - 1 = 63 ≥ 60`.
-/

namespace Physics.NFSClosure

open Module

variable {K : Type*} [Field K] {r c : ℕ}

/-- The space of left dependencies of a relation matrix `M` (rows = relations): vectors
`v` with `v ᵥ* M = 0`, realised as the kernel of `Mᵀ` acting on column vectors. -/
noncomputable def leftKernel (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) K) : Submodule K (Fin r → K) :=
  LinearMap.ker M.transpose.mulVecLin

/-- The left nullity: the number of independent dependencies Gaussian elimination finds. -/
noncomputable def leftNullity (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) K) : ℕ :=
  finrank K (leftKernel M)

theorem mem_leftKernel_iff (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) K) (v : Fin r → K) :
    v ∈ leftKernel M ↔ Matrix.vecMul v M = 0 := by
  simp [leftKernel]

/-- **Rank–nullity for relations.**  `rank M + leftNullity M = r`. -/
theorem rank_add_leftNullity (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) K) :
    M.rank + leftNullity M = r := by
  have h := LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker M.transpose.mulVecLin
  rw [Module.finrank_fin_fun] at h
  rw [← Matrix.rank_transpose]
  exact h

/-- **Excess guarantee.**  A relation matrix with `r` rows and `c` columns has at least
`r - c` independent left dependencies. -/
theorem excess_le_leftNullity (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) K) : r - c ≤ leftNullity M := by
  have h := rank_add_leftNullity M
  have hr : M.rank ≤ c := by
    simpa using M.rank_le_card_width
  omega

/-- Over `𝔽₂` the left kernel has exactly `2 ^ leftNullity` elements. -/
theorem card_leftKernel_GF2 (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) (ZMod 2)) :
    Nat.card (leftKernel M) = 2 ^ leftNullity M := by
  rw [leftNullity, Module.natCard_eq_pow_finrank (K := ZMod 2), Nat.card_zmod]

/-- Over `𝔽₂`, at least `2 ^ (r - c) - 1` nonzero dependency vectors exist. -/
theorem nonzero_dependencies_GF2 (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) (ZMod 2)) :
    2 ^ (r - c) - 1 ≤ Nat.card (leftKernel M) - 1 := by
  rw [card_leftKernel_GF2]
  have := Nat.pow_le_pow_right (by norm_num : 0 < 2) (excess_le_leftNullity M)
  omega

/-- A truncated instrument: it reports `min k n` where `n` is the true count. -/
def truncate (k n : ℕ) : ℕ := min k n

/-- **Saturation.**  The truncated dependency reading equals the cap `k` on every matrix
whose excess `r - c` reaches `k`. -/
theorem truncated_reading_saturates (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) K) {k : ℕ}
    (hk : k ≤ r - c) : truncate k (leftNullity M) = k := by
  have := excess_le_leftNullity M
  unfold truncate
  omega

/-- **Blindness.**  Two relation matrices (of possibly different shapes and over the same
field), both with excess at least `k`, produce identical truncated readings, regardless of
their actual nullities. -/
theorem truncated_reading_blind {r' c' : ℕ} (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) K)
    (M' : Matrix (Fin r') (Fin c') K) {k : ℕ} (hk : k ≤ r - c) (hk' : k ≤ r' - c') :
    truncate k (leftNullity M) = truncate k (leftNullity M') := by
  rw [truncated_reading_saturates M hk, truncated_reading_saturates M' hk']

/-- The truncated instrument is not injective on true nullities above the cap: it collapses
nullities `k` and `k + 1` (and every larger one) to the same value. -/
theorem truncate_not_injective (k : ℕ) : truncate k k = truncate k (k + 1) := by
  unfold truncate; omega

/-- **Round-44 instance.**  With cap `60`, any `𝔽₂` relation matrix carrying an excess of at
least `60` relations reads exactly `60`. -/
theorem left_dependencies_cap60 (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) (ZMod 2)) (h : 60 ≤ r - c) :
    truncate 60 (leftNullity M) = 60 :=
  truncated_reading_saturates M h

/-- **Vector-count variant.**  If the instrument counts *nonzero dependency vectors* (all
subset-products that are squares) rather than independent ones, the cap `60` is reached as
soon as the excess is `6`, because `2 ^ 6 - 1 = 63`. -/
theorem truncated_vector_count_saturates (M : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin c) (ZMod 2))
    (h : 6 ≤ r - c) : truncate 60 (Nat.card (leftKernel M) - 1) = 60 := by
  have h1 := nonzero_dependencies_GF2 M
  have h2 : 2 ^ 6 ≤ 2 ^ (r - c) := Nat.pow_le_pow_right (by norm_num) h
  unfold truncate
  omega

end Physics.NFSClosure
